newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION-Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup: Race debate.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION-Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup: Race debate.

text.p: By Russell Barton (ABC TV Political Editor)
You could tell the Government realised it had made a mistake in letting the race debate go on far too long -- everyone from the Prime Minister down started shooting the messenger.
John Howard turned his guns on the Asian media for the widespread coverage and critical editorials surrounding the Pauline Hanson furore.

Alexander Downer was in charge of lambasting the local coverage. Before and after an ABC raido interview on Wednesday morning the Foreign Minister attacked the "media beat-up" which he claims has taken place since Pauline Hanson made her maiden speech seven weeks ago. He shouted, he pounded the desk. But when interviewed he uttered the direct condemnation of Hanson which the Prmie Minister had studiously avoided. "Offensive and grotesque" was his description of her views.

Pity that Howard hadn't brought himself to a similar line weeks ago. The important questions out of this unseemly debate are: Why did Howard allow this to go on so long before he joined with Opposition Leader Kim Beazley in the joint motion to the Parliament on Wednesday afternoon; what does it say about his leadership; and is there any lasting stain?

Despite the media beat-up allegations, the coverage of Hanson's first speech to Parliament, riddled as it was with inaccuracies, was certainly not universal. Not all television news outlets put it to air. Newspaper coverage was scattered. The debate did not really build up a head of steam until the political leaders were asked for their reaction.

Kim Beazley took three weeks before he directly denounced her views. John Howard wouldn't comment at all. In fact to this day he still hasn't directly repudiated the Hanson manifesto, if it can be called that. Along the way he kept repeating one of his favourite lines; that we should be able to have a mature debate about immigration. As has been pointed out before, this goes back to 1988 when his decision to put a toe in the hot water of the Asian immigration debate unleashed a wave of criticism against him and provided rich growth conditions for a move against his leadership, which eventually succeeded in 1989.

Howard also is careful to steer away from any action which may be likened to the style of Paul Keating. The former Prime Minister would have wasted little time in putting the verbal boot into Hanson, probably at some electoral cost. (As if to prove the point, yesterday -- and characteristically from Jakarta -- Keating did speak up -- only his second intervention in domestic politics since his defeat.)
But Howard let it go. The longer he did so the more attention was directed to him. In political terms, it became Howard, rather than Hanson, who kept the story running at home.

And that's what made it news in Asia. The Prime Minister's failure to directly scotch Hanson's views translated into several Asian languages that he shared her views. Howard responded with his attack that the reports and editorials were written in ignorance of his repeated statements that he was committed to a non-discriminatory immigration policy.

This was answering the wrong question. What the media -- local and Asian -- were still looking for was the direct denunciation of Hanson's speech. As the week wore on it was clearer the debate had bolted. Howard's office ordered negotiations with the Opposition he stepped up on the joint motion to Parliament. The talks had been going on for more than two weeks since Kim Beazley invited Howard to join a motion he'd drafted.

Both sides believe the motion will be a circuit breaker. Tell that to the tourism industry which revealed on Wednesday it was all too late; five Asian tour groups had cancelled their Australian trips. This is just the tip of the iceberg. Business groups are emerging daily decrying the Hanson impact on business with Asia.

And Pauline Hanson refuses to be cowed. After ducking the debate over the joint motion (claiming she had another appointment which turned out to be for the following morning), she then popped up on the adjournment debate yesterday with a cleverly-constructed response to the motion. Acknowledging she was the target, she then agreed with much of it. The extreme elements of her maiden speech were watered down. She then called for a referendum on immigration, claiming she was simply wanted "a balance".

That speech should have rung further warning bells to Howard. Hanson's advisor, John Pasquarelli, is trying to take the rough edges off her presentation. This makes her most likely to be a longer-term proposition.

Howard's ultra-cautious approach to the problem -- now a feature of his leadership -- is not the answer. Canberra will have to back up the joint resolution with a constant barrage against the Hanson agenda, no matter what the electoral cost. Kim Beazley believes Hanson already is costing Labor up to three percent in votes, but he's prepared to continue to speak out against her.

In Government ranks, Tim Fischer has stood out for the strength of his language. He left on another Asian trade trip this morning. The information he brings back could be crucial to the Government's handling of the Hanson phenomenum.
(Opinions are those of the author, not those of Reuters)
